title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Agricultural Systems, or Those Systems of Political Economy That Treat the Produce of Land as Either the Sole or the Principal Source of Every Country's Revenue and Wealth
The agricultural systems of political economy will not need as long an explanation as the one I thought necessary to give the mercantile or commercial system.

As far as I know, no nation has ever adopted the system that treats the produce of land as the sole source of a country's revenue and wealth. At present it exists only in the theories of a few very learned and ingenious men in France. Surely it would not be worth examining at length the errors of a system that has never done, and probably never will do, any harm anywhere in the world. Still, I will try to lay out the broad outlines of this very ingenious system as clearly as I can.

Mr Colbert, the famous minister of Lewis XIV, was a man of integrity, great diligence, and command of detail. He had wide experience and a sharp eye for examining public accounts, and in short he had every ability needed to bring method and good order into the collection and spending of public revenue. Unfortunately, that minister had taken on all the prejudices of the mercantile system, which is by its very nature a system of restraint and regulation. Such a system could hardly fail to appeal to a hard-working, plodding man of business, used to managing the various departments of public offices and setting up the checks and controls needed to keep each one within its proper sphere. He tried to regulate the industry and commerce of a great country on the same model as the departments of a public office. Instead of letting every man pursue his own interest in his own way, on the liberal plan of equality, liberty, and justice, he granted special privileges to certain branches of industry while loading others with equally special restraints. Like other European ministers, he was inclined to favour the industry of the towns over that of the countryside; but he went further, and to prop up the towns' industry he was willing even to suppress and hold down that of the country. To make provisions cheap for townspeople, and so encourage manufactures and foreign trade, he banned the export of corn altogether, and thereby shut country people out of every foreign market for by far the most important part of what they produced. This ban, combined with the old provincial laws of France that restricted moving corn from one province to another, and with the arbitrary and degrading taxes levied on cultivators in almost every province, discouraged and held down French agriculture far below the level it would naturally have reached in such fertile soil and such a favourable climate. This state of discouragement and depression was felt to some degree in every part of the country, and many separate inquiries were launched into its causes. One of those causes appeared to be the preference that Mr Colbert's institutions gave to the industry of the towns over that of the country.

If a rod has been bent too far one way, the proverb says, you have to bend it just as far the other way to make it straight. The French philosophers who put forward the system that treats agriculture as the sole source of every country's revenue and wealth seem to have adopted this proverbial rule. Just as Mr Colbert's plan certainly overvalued the industry of the towns compared with that of the country, so their system seems to undervalue it just as surely.

They divide the different orders of people who have ever been supposed to contribute in any way to the country's yearly produce of land and labour into three classes. The first is the class of landowners. The second is the class of cultivators, farmers, and country labourers, whom they honour with the special name of the productive class. The third is the class of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants, whom they try to demean with the humiliating name of the barren or unproductive class.

The class of proprietors contributes to the yearly produce through whatever they may spend from time to time on improving the land: the buildings, drains, fences, and other betterments they make or maintain on it. By these means, the cultivators are able to raise a greater produce with the same capital, and so to pay a greater rent. This higher rent can be seen as the interest or profit due to the proprietor on the money or capital he puts into improving his land. In this system such outlays are called ground expenses (dépenses foncières).

The cultivators or farmers contribute to the yearly produce through what this system calls original and annual expenses (dépenses primitives et dépenses annuelles), which they lay out on cultivating the land. The original expenses consist of farming tools, the stock of cattle, the seed, and the upkeep of the farmer's family, servants, and cattle during at least a large part of the first year of his tenancy, or until he can get some return from the land. The annual expenses consist of seed, the wear and tear on farming tools, and the yearly upkeep of the farmer's servants and cattle, and of his family too, so far as any of them can be counted as servants employed in cultivation. The part of the land's produce that remains to him after paying the rent ought to be enough, first, to repay him within a reasonable time, at least during his tenancy, the whole of his original expenses together with the ordinary profits of stock; and, second, to repay him each year the whole of his annual expenses, again together with the ordinary profits of stock. These two kinds of expense are two capitals that the farmer employs in cultivation. Unless they are regularly returned to him along with a reasonable profit, he cannot carry on his business on equal terms with other businesses; and, looking to his own interest, he must abandon it as soon as he can and seek some other. The part of the land's produce that is thus needed to let the farmer continue his business ought to be regarded as a fund set aside and sacred to cultivation. If the landlord violates it, he necessarily reduces the produce of his own land, and within a few years he leaves the farmer unable not only to pay this excessive rent but even to pay the reasonable rent he might otherwise have got for the land. The rent that properly belongs to the landlord is no more than the net produce left over after fully paying all the necessary expenses that must first be laid out in order to raise the gross or total produce. It is because the cultivators' labour, over and above completely covering all those necessary expenses, yields a net produce of this kind that this system singles out this class of people with the honourable name of the productive class. For the same reason their original and annual expenses are called, in this system, productive expenses, because, beyond replacing their own value, they bring about the yearly reproduction of this net produce.

The ground expenses, as they are called, or what the landlord spends on improving his land, are in this system also honoured with the name of productive expenses. Until the whole of those expenses, together with the ordinary profits of stock, have been completely repaid to him through the higher rent he gets from his land, that higher rent ought to be treated as sacred and inviolable by both the church and the king, and ought to be subject neither to tithe nor to taxation. Otherwise, by discouraging the improvement of land, the church discourages the future growth of her own tithes, and the king the future growth of his own taxes. So, in a well-ordered state of things, since these ground expenses not only reproduce their own value completely but also, after a certain time, bring about the reproduction of a net produce, this system counts them as productive expenses.

The landlord's ground expenses, however, together with the farmer's original and annual expenses, are the only three kinds of expense that this system counts as productive. All other expenses, and all other orders of people, even those whom ordinary people regard as the most productive, are treated in this account as wholly barren and unproductive.

Artisans and manufacturers in particular, whose work, in ordinary people's view, adds so much to the value of the raw produce of land, are represented in this system as a class wholly barren and unproductive. Their labour, it is said, only replaces the stock that employs them, together with its ordinary profits. That stock consists of the materials, tools, and wages advanced to them by their employer; it is the fund set aside for their employment and upkeep. Its profits are the fund set aside for the upkeep of their employer. As the employer advances to them the stock of materials, tools, and wages they need for their work, so he also advances to himself what he needs for his own upkeep; and he generally sets that upkeep in proportion to the profit he expects to make from the price of their work. Unless the price repays him both the upkeep he advances to himself and the materials, tools, and wages he advances to his workmen, it clearly does not repay him the whole expense he lays out on it. So the profits of manufacturing stock are not, like the rent of land, a net produce that remains after fully repaying the whole expense that must be laid out in order to obtain it. The farmer's stock yields him a profit, just as the master manufacturer's does; and it also yields a rent to another person, which the master manufacturer's stock does not. The expense laid out in employing and maintaining artisans and manufacturers therefore does no more than keep its own value in existence, so to speak, and produces no new value. It is therefore an altogether barren and unproductive expense. The expense laid out in employing farmers and country labourers, by contrast, not only keeps its own value in existence but produces a new value, the landlord's rent. It is therefore a productive expense.

Mercantile stock is just as barren and unproductive as manufacturing stock. It merely keeps its own value in existence, without producing any new value. Its profits are only the repayment of the upkeep that its employer advances to himself during the time he employs it, or until he gets the returns from it. They are only the repayment of part of the expense that must be laid out in employing it.

The labour of artisans and manufacturers never adds anything to the value of the whole yearly amount of the land's raw produce. It does, indeed, add a great deal to the value of certain particular parts of it. But the consumption it causes of other parts in the meantime is exactly equal to the value it adds to those parts, so that the value of the whole amount is not, at any single moment, increased in the least by it. The person who makes the lace for a pair of fine ruffles, for example, will sometimes raise the value of perhaps a pennyworth of flax to £30 sterling. But although at first glance he seems thereby to multiply the value of part of the raw produce about seven thousand two hundred times, he in fact adds nothing to the value of the whole yearly amount of the raw produce. Making that lace costs him perhaps two years' labour. The £30 he gets for it when it is finished is no more than the repayment of the subsistence he advances to himself during the two years he spends on it. The value he adds to the flax by each day's, month's, or year's labour does no more than replace the value of his own consumption during that day, month, or year. So at no moment does he add anything to the value of the whole yearly amount of the land's raw produce: the portion of that produce he is continually consuming is always equal to the value he is continually producing. The extreme poverty of most of the people employed in this expensive though trifling manufacture may convince us that the price of their work does not, in the usual case, exceed the value of their subsistence. It is otherwise with the work of farmers and country labourers. The landlord's rent is a value that, in the usual case, their work is continually producing over and above completely replacing the whole consumption, the whole expense laid out on employing and maintaining both the workmen and their employer.

Artisans, manufacturers, and merchants can increase the revenue and wealth of their society only by thrift, or, as this system puts it, by privation, that is, by depriving themselves of part of the funds set aside for their own subsistence. Each year they reproduce nothing but those funds. So unless they save some part of them each year, unless they deny themselves the enjoyment of some part of them each year, the revenue and wealth of their society can never be increased in the slightest by their work. Farmers and country labourers, by contrast, can fully enjoy all the funds set aside for their own subsistence and yet at the same time increase the revenue and wealth of their society. Over and above what is set aside for their own subsistence, their work yields each year a net produce, and any growth in it necessarily increases the revenue and wealth of their society. So nations that, like France or England, consist largely of proprietors and cultivators can be enriched both by work and by enjoyment. Nations that, like Holland and Hamburg, are made up chiefly of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers can grow rich only through thrift and privation. Because the interests of nations in such different situations are very different, so too is the common character of the people. In nations of the first kind, generosity, frankness, and good fellowship naturally form part of the common character; in those of the second kind, narrowness, meanness, and a selfish disposition averse to all social pleasure and enjoyment.

The unproductive class, that of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, is wholly maintained and employed at the expense of the other two classes, the proprietors and the cultivators. These supply it with both the materials of its work and the fund of its subsistence, the corn and cattle it consumes while it is engaged in that work. In the end the proprietors and cultivators pay both the wages of all the workmen of the unproductive class and the profits of all their employers. Those workmen and their employers are really the servants of the proprietors and cultivators. They are merely servants who work out of doors, as menial servants work indoors. Both, however, are equally maintained at the expense of the same masters. The labour of both is equally unproductive. It adds nothing to the value of the total raw produce of the land. Instead of increasing the value of that total, it is a charge and an expense that has to be paid out of it.

The unproductive class, however, is not just useful but greatly useful to the other two classes. Through the work of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, the proprietors and cultivators can buy both the foreign goods and the manufactured produce of their own country that they need, using the produce of far less of their own labour than they would have to spend if they tried, in a clumsy and unskilled way, either to import the one or to make the other for their own use. Through the unproductive class, the cultivators are freed from many cares that would otherwise distract their attention from cultivating the land. The greater produce they are able to raise as a result of this undivided attention is more than enough to pay the whole cost that maintaining and employing the unproductive class imposes on either the proprietors or themselves. So the work of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers, though in its own nature wholly unproductive, contributes in this way indirectly to increasing the produce of the land. It increases the productive powers of productive labour by leaving it free to confine itself to its proper task, the cultivation of land; and the plough often goes the easier and the better thanks to the labour of the man whose business is most remote from the plough.

It can never be in the interest of the proprietors and cultivators to restrain or discourage in any way the work of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers. The greater the freedom this unproductive class enjoys, the greater the competition will be in all the different trades that make it up, and the more cheaply the other two classes will be supplied with both foreign goods and the manufactured produce of their own country.

It can never be in the interest of the unproductive class to oppress the other two classes. It is the surplus produce of the land, what remains after subtracting the upkeep first of the cultivators and then of the proprietors, that maintains and employs the unproductive class. The greater this surplus, the greater the maintenance and employment of that class must likewise be. Establishing perfect justice, perfect liberty, and perfect equality is the very simple secret that most effectively secures the highest degree of prosperity for all three classes.

The merchants, artisans, and manufacturers of those mercantile states that, like Holland and Hamburg, consist chiefly of this unproductive class are in the same way wholly maintained and employed at the expense of the proprietors and cultivators of land. The only difference is that most of those proprietors and cultivators are placed at a most inconvenient distance from the merchants, artisans, and manufacturers they supply with the materials of their work and the fund of their subsistence: they are inhabitants of other countries and subjects of other governments.

Such mercantile states, however, are not merely useful but greatly useful to the inhabitants of those other countries. They fill, to some extent, a very important gap, and take the place of the merchants, artisans, and manufacturers that the inhabitants of those countries ought to find at home, but, through some flaw in their policy, do not find at home.

It can never be in the interest of those landed nations, if I may call them that, to discourage or distress the work of such mercantile states by imposing high duties on their trade or on the goods they supply. By making those goods dearer, such duties could only sink the real value of the surplus produce of the landed nations' own land, with which, or, what amounts to the same thing, with the price of which, those goods are bought. Such duties could only serve to discourage the growth of that surplus produce, and consequently the improvement and cultivation of their own land. The most effective course, on the contrary, for raising the value of that surplus produce, for encouraging its growth, and so for improving and cultivating their own land, would be to allow the most perfect freedom to the trade of all such mercantile nations.

This perfect freedom of trade would even be the most effective means of supplying them, in due course, with all the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants they lacked at home, and of filling, in the most fitting and advantageous way, that very important gap they felt there.

The continual growth of the surplus produce of their land would, in due course, create a greater capital than could be employed at the ordinary rate of profit in improving and cultivating land; and the surplus part of it would naturally turn to employing artisans and manufacturers at home. But these artisans and manufacturers, finding at home both the materials of their work and the fund of their subsistence, might at once, even with far less art and skill, be able to work as cheaply as the small-scale artisans and manufacturers of such mercantile states, who had to bring both from a greater distance. Even if, for lack of art and skill, they could not for a time work as cheaply, yet, having a market at home, they might be able to sell their work there as cheaply as that of the artisans and manufacturers of such mercantile states, which could be brought to that market only from so great a distance; and as their art and skill improved, they would soon be able to sell it more cheaply. So the artisans and manufacturers of such mercantile states would at once meet rivals in the market of those landed nations, and soon after be undersold and pushed out of it altogether. The cheapness of the manufactures of those landed nations, resulting from the gradual improvement of art and skill, would in due course extend their sales beyond the home market and carry them to many foreign markets, from which they would, in the same way, gradually push out many of the manufacturers of such mercantile nations.

This continual growth, in both the raw and the manufactured produce of those landed nations, would in due course create a greater capital than could be employed, at the ordinary rate of profit, either in agriculture or in manufactures. The surplus of this capital would naturally turn to foreign trade and be used to export to foreign countries whatever parts of the raw and manufactured produce of its own country exceeded the demand of the home market. In exporting the produce of their own country, the merchants of a landed nation would have an advantage of the same kind over those of mercantile nations as its artisans and manufacturers had over the artisans and manufacturers of such nations: the advantage of finding at home the cargo, and the stores and provisions, that the others were obliged to seek from a distance. So, even with inferior art and skill in navigation, they would be able to sell that cargo as cheaply in foreign markets as the merchants of such mercantile nations, and with equal art and skill they would be able to sell it more cheaply. They would therefore soon rival those mercantile nations in this branch of foreign trade, and in due course push them out of it altogether.

According to this liberal and generous system, then, the most advantageous way for a landed nation to raise up artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of its own is to grant the most perfect freedom of trade to the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of all other nations. In this way it raises the value of the surplus produce of its own land, whose continual growth gradually builds up a fund that, in due course, necessarily raises up all the artisans, manufacturers, and merchants it needs.

When a landed nation, on the contrary, oppresses the trade of foreign nations, whether by high duties or by outright bans, it necessarily harms its own interest in two ways. First, by raising the price of all foreign goods and all kinds of manufactures, it necessarily sinks the real value of the surplus produce of its own land, with which, or, what amounts to the same thing, with the price of which, it buys those foreign goods and manufactures. Second, by giving its own merchants, artisans, and manufacturers a kind of monopoly of the home market, it raises the rate of mercantile and manufacturing profit relative to that of agricultural profit, and consequently either draws away from agriculture part of the capital that had been employed in it, or stops part of what would otherwise have gone to it from going there. So this policy discourages agriculture in two ways: first, by sinking the real value of its produce and thereby lowering the rate of its profits; and, second, by raising the rate of profit in all other occupations. Agriculture is made less advantageous, and trade and manufactures more advantageous, than they otherwise would be; and every man is tempted by his own interest to turn as much of his capital and his work as he can away from the former and toward the latter.

Even supposing this oppressive policy enabled a landed nation to raise up artisans, manufacturers, and merchants of its own somewhat sooner than it could through freedom of trade, which is itself far from certain, it would still raise them up, so to speak, prematurely, before the nation was fully ready for them. By raising up one kind of industry too hastily, it would depress another, more valuable kind. By raising up too hastily a kind of industry that merely replaces the stock that employs it, together with the ordinary profit, it would depress a kind of industry that, beyond replacing that stock with its profit, also yields a net produce, a free rent to the landlord. It would depress productive labour by encouraging too hastily that labour which is wholly barren and unproductive.

How, according to this system, the total yearly produce of the land is distributed among the three classes mentioned above, and how the labour of the unproductive class does no more than replace the value of its own consumption without increasing in any way the value of that total, is set out by Mr Quesnai, the very ingenious and profound author of this system, in some arithmetical tables. The first of these, which he singles out by way of distinction with the name of the Economical Table, shows the way he supposes this distribution to take place in a state of the most perfect liberty, and therefore of the highest prosperity; a state in which the yearly produce is such as to afford the greatest possible net produce, and in which each class enjoys its proper share of the whole yearly produce. Some later tables show the way he supposes this distribution is made under various states of restraint and regulation, in which either the class of proprietors or the barren and unproductive class is favoured more than the class of cultivators, and in which one or the other encroaches, more or less, on the share that ought properly to belong to this productive class. According to this system, every such encroachment, every violation of the natural distribution that perfect liberty would establish, must necessarily degrade, more or less, from one year to the next, the value and total of the yearly produce, and must necessarily cause a gradual decline in the real wealth and revenue of society; a decline whose progress must be quicker or slower according to the degree of the encroachment, according as the natural distribution that perfect liberty would establish is more or less violated. Those later tables show the different degrees of decline that, according to this system, correspond to the different degrees in which this natural distribution of things is violated.

Some speculative physicians seem to have imagined that the health of the human body could be preserved only by a certain precise regimen of diet and exercise, and that every violation of it, however small, necessarily caused some degree of disease or disorder in proportion to the violation. Experience, however, seems to show that the human body often keeps, to all appearances at least, the most perfect state of health under a vast variety of different regimens, even some generally believed to be very far from wholesome. The healthy human body, it seems, contains within itself some unknown principle of preservation, able in many respects either to prevent or to correct the bad effects even of a very faulty regimen. Mr Quesnai, who was himself a physician, and a very speculative one, seems to have held a notion of the same kind about the body politic, imagining that it would thrive and prosper only under a certain precise regimen, the exact regimen of perfect liberty and perfect justice. He seems not to have considered that in the body politic the natural effort each man is continually making to better his own condition is a principle of preservation, able in many respects to prevent and correct the bad effects of a political economy that is to some degree both partial and oppressive. Such a political economy, though it no doubt retards more or less, is not always able to halt altogether the natural progress of a nation toward wealth and prosperity, and still less able to make it go backwards. If a nation could not prosper without enjoying perfect liberty and perfect justice, there is not a nation in the world that could ever have prospered. In the body politic, however, the wisdom of nature has fortunately made ample provision for remedying many of the bad effects of the folly and injustice of man, just as it has done in the natural body for remedying those of his sloth and intemperance.

The fundamental error of this system, however, seems to lie in its treating the class of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants as wholly barren and unproductive. The following observations may serve to show how improper this representation is:—

First, this class, it is acknowledged, reproduces each year the value of its own yearly consumption, and at least keeps in existence the stock or capital that maintains and employs it. But on that ground alone the name barren or unproductive seems very improperly applied to it. We would not call a marriage barren or unproductive even if it produced only a son and a daughter to replace the father and mother, and did not increase the number of the human species but only kept it as it was before. Farmers and country labourers, it is true, over and above the stock that maintains and employs them, reproduce each year a net produce, a free rent for the landlord. Just as a marriage that yields three children is certainly more productive than one that yields only two, so the labour of farmers and country labourers is certainly more productive than that of merchants, artisans, and manufacturers. But the greater produce of the one class does not make the other barren or unproductive.

Second, on this same ground it seems altogether improper to regard artisans, manufacturers, and merchants in the same light as menial servants. The labour of menial servants does not keep in existence the fund that maintains and employs them. Their upkeep and employment is wholly at their masters' expense, and the work they do is not of a kind to repay that expense. That work consists in services that generally perish in the very instant they are performed, and does not fix or realize itself in any saleable commodity that can replace the value of their wages and upkeep. The labour of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants, by contrast, naturally does fix and realize itself in some such saleable commodity. It is on this account that, in the chapter where I deal with productive and unproductive labour, I have classed artisans, manufacturers, and merchants among the productive labourers, and menial servants among the barren or unproductive.

Third, on every supposition it seems improper to say that the labour of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants does not increase the real revenue of society. Even if we supposed, as this system seems to suppose, that the value of this class's daily, monthly, and yearly consumption was exactly equal to that of its daily, monthly, and yearly production, it would not follow that its labour added nothing to the real revenue, to the real value of the yearly produce of the land and labour of society. An artisan, for example, who in the first six months after harvest does ten pounds' worth of work, even though in the same time he consumes ten pounds' worth of corn and other necessaries, really adds ten pounds of value to the yearly produce of the land and labour of society. While he has been consuming a half-yearly revenue of ten pounds' worth of corn and other necessaries, he has produced an equal value of work, able to buy, either for himself or for someone else, an equal half-yearly revenue. So the value of what has been consumed and produced during these six months is equal not to ten but to twenty pounds. It is possible, indeed, that no more than ten pounds' worth of this value ever existed at any single moment. But if the ten pounds' worth of corn and other necessaries consumed by the artisan had instead been consumed by a soldier or a menial servant, the value of that part of the yearly produce existing at the end of the six months would have been ten pounds less than it actually is thanks to the artisan's labour. So even though the value of what the artisan produces is supposed never, at any single moment, to be greater than the value he consumes, yet at every moment the value of goods actually existing in the market is, because of what he produces, greater than it otherwise would be.

When the supporters of this system claim that the consumption of artisans, manufacturers, and merchants is equal to the value of what they produce, they probably mean no more than that their revenue, or the fund set aside for their consumption, is equal to it. But if they had expressed themselves more accurately, and claimed only that the revenue of this class was equal to the value of what it produced, the reader might readily have noticed that whatever was naturally saved out of this revenue must necessarily increase, more or less, the real wealth of society. So in order to construct something like an argument, they had to express themselves as they did; and this argument, even granting that things were as it seems to assume, turns out to be a very weak one.

Fourth, farmers and country labourers can no more increase, without thrift, the real revenue, the yearly produce of the land and labour of their society, than artisans, manufacturers, and merchants can. The yearly produce of the land and labour of any society can be increased in only two ways: first, by some improvement in the productive powers of the useful labour actually maintained within it; or, second, by some increase in the quantity of that labour.

The improvement in the productive powers of useful labour depends, first, on improvement in the workman's skill, and, second, on improvement in the machinery he works with. But the labour of artisans and manufacturers, since it can be more finely subdivided, and the labour of each workman reduced to a greater simplicity of operation, than that of farmers and country labourers, is likewise capable of both these kinds of improvement to a much higher degree (see book i, chap. 1). In this respect, therefore, the class of cultivators can have no sort of advantage over that of artisans and manufacturers.

How much useful labour a society actually employs depends entirely on how much its capital grows, and that capital can grow only by exactly the amount saved out of revenue—whether saved by the people who manage and direct the capital themselves, or by others who lend it to them. This system assumes that merchants, craftsmen, and manufacturers are naturally more thrifty and more inclined to save than landowners and farmers. If that is true, then to that extent they are the ones more likely to expand the useful labour employed in their society, and so to increase its real revenue, which is the yearly output of its land and labour.

Fifth and finally: even if we grant this system's assumption that a country's revenue consists entirely of the amount of subsistence its industry can secure, a trading and manufacturing country must still always be far richer than one without trade or manufactures, all else being equal. Trade and manufactures let a country import more subsistence each year than its own land, cultivated as it currently is, could supply. Townspeople often own no land at all, yet through their industry they draw to themselves enough of the raw produce of other people's land to supply both the materials of their work and the fund that feeds them. What a town always is to the countryside around it, one independent state can often be to other independent states. This is how Holland draws much of its food from abroad—live cattle from Holstein and Jutland, and grain from almost every country in Europe. A small amount of manufactured goods buys a large amount of raw produce. So a trading and manufacturing country naturally uses a small part of its manufactured output to buy a large part of the raw produce of other countries, while a country without trade or manufactures must usually give up a large part of its raw produce to buy only a tiny part of other countries' manufactured goods. The first exports what can support and supply only a few people, and imports the support and supply of many. The second exports the support and supply of many, and imports that of only a few. The people of the first must always enjoy far more subsistence than their own land, as currently cultivated, could provide. The people of the second must always enjoy far less.

Still, for all its flaws, this system is perhaps the closest approach to the truth yet published on the subject of political economy, and for that reason it deserves the attention of anyone who wants to study the principles of that very important science carefully. Its claim that only labour applied to land is productive is, admittedly, too narrow and cramped. But when it says that the wealth of nations lies not in the useless hoard of money but in the consumable goods that the society's labour reproduces each year, and when it says that perfect liberty is the only effective way to make that yearly reproduction as large as possible, its doctrine seems entirely as sound as it is generous and liberal. Its followers are very numerous. Because people love paradoxes and love seeming to grasp what is beyond ordinary minds, the paradox it defends—that manufacturing labour is unproductive—has probably done a fair bit to swell its ranks of admirers. For some years now they have formed a sizeable sect, known in the French literary world as the Economists. Their writings have certainly done their country some good, both by opening up many subjects to general discussion that had never been properly examined before, and by nudging public policy somewhat in favour of agriculture. It is thanks to their arguments that French agriculture has been freed from several of the burdens it once laboured under. The term for which a lease can be granted so as to hold good against any future buyer or owner of the land has been extended from nine years to twenty-seven. The old provincial barriers on moving grain from one province of the kingdom to another have been wholly removed, and the freedom to export grain to all foreign countries has been made the common law of the kingdom in all ordinary cases. This sect's writings are very numerous, and they deal not only with what is properly called political economy—the nature and causes of the wealth of nations—but with every other branch of civil government, and in all of them the authors follow the doctrine of Mr Qttesnai faithfully and without any noticeable variation. Because of this, most of their works show little variety. The clearest and best-organized account of the doctrine is in a small book by Mr Mercier de la Riviere, formerly intendant of Martinico, called The Natural and Essential Order of Political Societies. The whole sect's admiration for their master—a man himself of the greatest modesty and simplicity—is no less than that of any of the ancient philosophers for the founders of their own systems. 'Since the world began,' says the diligent and respected Marquis de Mirabeau, 'there have been three great inventions that have chiefly given stability to political societies, apart from the many others that have enriched and adorned them. The first is the invention of writing, which alone gives human nature the power to pass on its laws, contracts, records, and discoveries without alteration. The second is the invention of money, which ties together all the relations among civilized societies. The third is the economical table, which grows out of the other two and completes them both by perfecting their purpose—the great discovery of our age, though it is our descendants who will reap its benefit.'

European nations in modern times have shaped their economic policy to favour manufactures and foreign trade—the industry of the towns—over agriculture, the industry of the country. Other nations have followed the opposite plan, favouring agriculture over manufactures and foreign trade.

China's policy favours agriculture above every other occupation. In China, a farm labourer is said to rank as far above a craftsman as, in most of Europe, a craftsman ranks above a labourer. Every man's great ambition there is to get hold of a small plot of land, whether as owner or as tenant, and leases are said to be granted on very moderate terms and well secured to the tenants. The Chinese have little regard for foreign trade. 'Your beggarly commerce!' was how the mandarins of Peking used to speak of it to Mr De Lange, the Russian envoy (see the Journal of Mr De Lange, in Bell's Travels, vol. ii, pp. 258, 276, 293). Except with Japan, the Chinese carry on little or no foreign trade themselves in their own ships, and they admit foreign ships to only one or two of their ports. So foreign trade in China is confined to a far narrower scope than it would naturally reach if it were given more freedom, whether in Chinese ships or in foreign ones.

Manufactured goods often pack great value into small bulk, so they can be shipped from one country to another more cheaply than most raw produce, and for that reason they are the main support of foreign trade almost everywhere. In countries smaller and less favourably placed for internal commerce than China, manufactures generally need the support of foreign trade. Without a large foreign market they can hardly thrive—either in countries too modest in size to offer more than a narrow home market, or in countries where travel between provinces is so hard that goods made in one place cannot reach the whole home market the country could otherwise provide. Remember that the perfection of manufacturing depends entirely on the division of labour, and that how far the division of labour can be carried in any trade is set, as already shown, by the extent of the market. But China's vast size, its enormous population, the range of climates and therefore of products across its provinces, and the easy water-transport linking most of them, make that country's home market so large that it alone can support very great manufactures and allow very considerable subdivision of labour. China's home market is perhaps not much smaller in extent than the markets of all the different countries of Europe combined. Even so, a wider foreign trade—one that added to this huge home market the foreign market of all the rest of the world, especially if a good part of it were carried in Chinese ships—could hardly fail to expand China's manufactures greatly and to improve the productive power of its manufacturing industry. With more extensive shipping, the Chinese would naturally learn to use and build for themselves all the various machines used in other countries, along with the other improvements in art and industry practised around the world. Under their present plan, they have little chance to improve themselves by any other nation's example, except that of the Japanese.
The policy of ancient Egypt, and that of the Gentoo government of Indostan, also seem to have favoured agriculture above every other occupation.

In both ancient Egypt and Indostan, the whole population was divided into castes or tribes, each of which was confined, from father to son, to a particular job or class of jobs. A priest's son was necessarily a priest, a soldier's son a soldier, a labourer's son a labourer, a weaver's son a weaver, a tailor's son a tailor, and so on. In both countries the caste of priests held the highest rank and that of soldiers the next; and in both the caste of farmers and labourers ranked above the castes of merchants and manufacturers.

The governments of both countries were especially attentive to the interest of agriculture. The works that the ancient sovereigns of Egypt built to distribute the waters of the Nile properly were famous in antiquity, and the ruined remains of some still astonish travellers. The works of the same kind built by the ancient sovereigns of Indostan to distribute the waters of the Ganges and many other rivers, though less celebrated, seem to have been just as great. Accordingly, both countries—though sometimes hit by famine—were famous for their great fertility. Both were extremely populous, yet in years of moderate plenty both could export large quantities of grain to their neighbours.

The ancient Egyptians had a superstitious dread of the sea, and since the Gentoo religion forbids its followers to light a fire, and so to cook any food, on the water, it effectively bars them from all long sea voyages. Both the Egyptians and the Indians must therefore have relied almost entirely on the ships of other nations to export their surplus produce, and this dependence, by confining their market, must have discouraged the growth of that surplus. It must have discouraged the growth of manufactured produce even more than that of raw produce, because manufactures need a far wider market than the most important kinds of raw produce do. A single shoemaker will make more than 300 pairs of shoes a year, while his own family will perhaps not wear out six pairs. So unless he has the custom of at least 50 families like his own, he cannot sell all that he makes. The largest class of craftsmen will rarely, in a big country, amount to more than one in 50 or one in 100 of all its families. But in large countries such as France and England, the number of people employed in agriculture has been put by some writers at a half, by others at a third, and by no writer I know of at less than a fifth of the whole population. Since almost all the produce of French and English agriculture is consumed at home, each person employed in it must, by these estimates, need little more than the custom of one, two, or at most four families like his own in order to sell all his output. Agriculture, then, can sustain itself far better than manufactures under the handicap of a confined market. In both ancient Egypt and Indostan, the narrowness of the foreign market was in some measure offset by the convenience of many inland waterways, which opened the whole home market, in the most advantageous way, to the produce of every district. The great size of Indostan also made its home market very large, enough to support a wide variety of manufactures. But ancient Egypt's small size—it was never as large as England—must always have made its home market too narrow to support much variety of manufactures. Accordingly Bengal, the province of Indostan that usually exports the most rice, has always been more notable for exporting a great variety of manufactures than for exporting its grain. Ancient Egypt, by contrast, though it exported some manufactures—fine linen in particular, along with some other goods—was always most famous for its great exports of grain. It was long the granary of the Roman empire.

The sovereigns of China, of ancient Egypt, and of the various kingdoms into which Indostan has at different times been divided have always drawn the whole, or by far the largest part, of their revenue from some kind of land tax or land rent. This land tax or land rent, like the tithe in Europe, consisted of a fixed share—a fifth, it is said—of the land's produce, paid either in kind or in money according to a set valuation, and so it varied from year to year with every variation in the crop. It was natural, then, for the sovereigns of those countries to take a special interest in agriculture, since the yearly rise or fall of their own revenue depended directly on whether it prospered or declined.

The policy of the ancient republics of Greece, and that of Rome, honoured agriculture above manufactures and foreign trade, but it seems to have discouraged those latter occupations rather than to have given agriculture any direct or deliberate encouragement. In several of the ancient Greek states foreign trade was banned outright; in several others the trades of craftsmen and manufacturers were held to harm the strength and agility of the body, to spoil it for the habits their military and gymnastic exercises tried to instil, and so to make it more or less unfit for bearing the hardships and facing the dangers of war. Such occupations were thought fit only for slaves, and the free citizens were forbidden to practise them. Even in states where there was no such ban, as in Rome and Athens, the bulk of the people were in effect shut out of all the trades now commonly carried on by the lower townsfolk. At Athens and Rome those trades were all worked by the slaves of the rich, who carried them on for their masters' profit; the masters' wealth, power, and protection made it nearly impossible for a poor freeman to find a market for his work when it had to compete with the work of the rich men's slaves. But slaves are very seldom inventive, and all the most important improvements in machinery, or in the arrangement and distribution of work, that make labour easier and quicker have been the discoveries of free men. If a slave were to suggest any such improvement, his master would very likely treat the suggestion as a sign of laziness and a wish to spare himself work at the master's expense. Instead of a reward, the poor slave would probably meet plenty of abuse and perhaps some punishment. So in manufactures run by slaves, more labour must generally have been spent to do the same amount of work than in those run by free men, and the slave's work must therefore generally have cost more than the free man's. Mr Montesquieu remarks that the Hungarian mines, though no richer, have always been worked at less expense, and so at more profit, than the Turkish mines nearby. The Turkish mines are worked by slaves, and those slaves' arms are the only machines the Turks have ever thought to use; the Hungarian mines are worked by free men, who employ a great deal of machinery to make their own labour easier and quicker. From the little we know about the price of manufactures in Greek and Roman times, the finer sorts appear to have been extremely dear. Silk sold for its weight in gold. It was not then a European manufacture, and since it all came from the East Indies, the distance of carriage may partly explain the high price. But the price a lady would sometimes pay, it is said, for a piece of very fine linen seems just as extravagant; and since linen was always a European, or at most an Egyptian, manufacture, this high price can only be explained by the great cost of the labour that went into it—and that cost of labour could come from nothing but the clumsiness of the machinery used. The price of fine woollens, too, though not quite so extravagant, seems to have been well above today's. Pliny tells us (Plin. l. ix, c. 39) that some cloths dyed in a particular way cost a hundred denarii, or £3 6s 8d, the pound weight, and others dyed another way cost a thousand denarii the pound weight, or £33 6s 8d. Remember that the Roman pound held only twelve of our avoirdupois ounces. This high price does seem to have been chiefly due to the dye. But unless the cloths themselves had been much dearer than any made today, so costly a dye would probably not have been used on them; the gap between the value of the accessory and that of the main item would have been too great. The price the same author mentions (Plin. l. viii, c. 48) for certain triclinaria—a kind of woollen pillow or cushion used for leaning on while reclining on couches at table—beggars belief; some are said to have cost more than £30,000, others more than £300,000, and in this case the high price is not put down to the dye. Dr Arbuthnot observes that the dress of fashionable people of both sexes seems to have shown much less variety in ancient than in modern times, and the very limited variety we see in ancient statues bears him out. He concludes that their dress must on the whole have been cheaper than ours, but the conclusion does not seem to follow. When fashionable dress is very expensive, the variety must be very small; but when improvements in manufacturing make the cost of any one outfit quite moderate, the variety naturally becomes very great. The rich, unable to set themselves apart by the cost of any single outfit, will naturally try to do so by the number and variety of their outfits.

The greatest and most important branch of every nation's commerce, as already noted, is the one carried on between townspeople and country people. The townspeople draw from the country the raw produce that supplies both the materials of their work and the fund that feeds them, and they pay for it by sending back to the country a portion of that produce manufactured and made ready for immediate use. So the trade between these two sets of people comes down in the end to a certain quantity of raw produce exchanged for a certain quantity of manufactured produce. The dearer the manufactured goods, then, the cheaper the raw produce; and whatever raises the price of manufactured produce in a country lowers the price of the land's raw produce, and so discourages agriculture. The smaller the quantity of manufactured produce that any given quantity of raw produce—or, what amounts to the same thing, the price of any given quantity of raw produce—can buy, the smaller the exchangeable value of that raw produce, and the less incentive the landlord has to increase it by improving his land or the farmer by cultivating it. And whatever reduces the number of craftsmen and manufacturers in a country reduces the home market—the most important of all markets—for the land's raw produce, and so discourages agriculture still further.

So those systems that, preferring agriculture to every other occupation, try to promote it by restraining manufactures and foreign trade actually work against their own aim and indirectly discourage the very kind of industry they mean to encourage. In this respect they are perhaps even more inconsistent than the mercantile system. The mercantile system, by encouraging manufactures and foreign trade over agriculture, diverts a certain share of the society's capital from a more profitable to a less profitable kind of industry—but in the end it really does encourage the kind of industry it means to promote. These agricultural systems, by contrast, really do discourage in the end the very kind of industry they favour.

Every system, then, that tries either to draw towards a particular kind of industry, by special encouragements, a larger share of the society's capital than would naturally go to it, or to force away from a particular kind of industry, by special restraints, some share of the capital that would otherwise be employed in it, in fact undermines the very purpose it means to serve. Instead of speeding the society's progress towards real wealth and greatness, it slows it; and instead of increasing the real value of the yearly output of its land and labour, it diminishes it.

Once all these systems of preference and restraint are completely swept away, the obvious and simple system of natural liberty establishes itself on its own. As long as a man does not break the laws of justice, he is left perfectly free to pursue his own interest in his own way and to bring his industry and capital into competition with those of any other man or group of men. The sovereign is wholly relieved of a duty that, in trying to perform it, would always leave him open to countless errors, and that no human wisdom or knowledge could ever perform properly—the duty of overseeing the industry of private people and directing it towards the occupations best suited to the society's interest. Under the system of natural liberty, the sovereign has only three duties to attend to—three duties of great importance, certainly, but plain and intelligible to ordinary minds. First, the duty of protecting the society from the violence and invasion of other independent societies. Second, the duty of protecting, as far as possible, every member of the society from the injustice or oppression of every other member—that is, the duty of maintaining an exact administration of justice. Third, the duty of building and maintaining certain public works and certain public institutions that it can never be in the interest of any individual, or small group of individuals, to build and maintain, because the profit could never repay the cost to any individual or small group, even though it may often more than repay it to a great society.

Performing these several duties of the sovereign properly necessarily involves a certain expense, and that expense in turn necessarily requires a certain revenue to support it. In the next book, then, I shall try to explain, first, what the necessary expenses of the sovereign or commonwealth are; which of those expenses ought to be met by the general contribution of the whole society, and which by that of only some particular part or particular members of it. Second, what the different methods are by which the whole society can be made to contribute towards meeting the expenses that fall on the whole society, and what the chief advantages and drawbacks of each method are. And third, what the reasons and causes are that have led almost all modern governments to mortgage part of this revenue, or to run up debts, and what effects those debts have had on the real wealth—the yearly output of the land and labour—of the society. The next book will therefore divide naturally into three chapters.
